chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
title: Memphis: marrying John, forming a union and the Lunceford friendship
summary: After Seymour died the group ended up in Memphis, where she married John Williams. He organised the musicians into a union, raising pay from $2 a night, and was a friend and checkers rival of Jimmy Lunceford.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Now, after New York you went back to Pittsburgh and then you went to Memphis?

I went to Memphis after Seymour died. We went with Seymour and Jeanette, his wife, for a while and we were stranded, as I said, and finally made it to Pittsburgh. Joe Williams - I left him there with my people, the guitar and banjo player.
Had you married John Williams at that time?
No, we got married in Memphis.

No, but they went to school together. Joe Williams was from Kansas City, Kansas; and John was from Memphis, Tennessee, but he went to school in Kansas City. That's where he met Joe. When we went to Memphis, Tennessee, that's where John Williams my husband - who later became my husband - was born and so we got in the band together. He was such a terrific man. The union musicians there - they had no union when I was there - he got a union going for them. The musicians would work like from 8 o'clock till 3 or 4 in the morning and they'd get

paid $2, so John, when he left Memphis they were making over $20-25 and the leader $30, because I remember once - they were very, very prejudiced in Memphis - he had such a terrific band and Jimmy Lunceford was teaching at a high school there. He and Jimmy Lunceford were very good friends (John Williams and Jimmy Lunceford). So everything that John did Jimmy would try to do something better. So he said to John, "I'm going to get a band better than that combo you have." Jimmy got himself a girl piano player and he taught kids - high school pupils, he was teaching in a high school - he taught them music. All these young kids being brought up in Memphis, he taught them music. He and John used to play checkers and John would beat him playing checkers and he'd say, "That's all right; I'm going to get a band better than you."
